title: Indexes: Speeding Up Lookups
what_is_it: An index is an extra, separately-stored structure that lets Postgres find matching rows without scanning the entire table - CREATE INDEX builds one on a column, CREATE UNIQUE INDEX also enforces no duplicates (the same mechanism a UNIQUE constraint uses internally), and DROP INDEX removes one.
why_it_matters: Without an index, a WHERE or JOIN condition on a column forces Postgres to check every single row (a sequential scan) - fine for a handful of rows, painfully slow once a table has millions. An index turns that into a near-instant lookup, at the cost of some extra disk space and slightly slower writes to that column.
output:
CREATE INDEX
(no rows returned - queries filtering on orders.customer_id can now use this index instead of scanning every row)
common_mistakes: Adding an index to every column 'just in case' - each index costs real disk space and slows down every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on that table, so indexes are worth adding for columns you actually filter, join, or sort on frequently, not reflexively everywhere. Also assuming DROP INDEX is risky - it never touches any data, only the lookup structure.
mini_exercise: Why does adding a UNIQUE constraint to a column (like earlier with products.name) automatically create an index for it too?
postgres_note: Postgres's default index type is B-tree, which handles equality and range comparisons (=, <, >, BETWEEN) well - other types (GIN for full-text search and arrays, GiST for geometric data) exist for specialized use cases.
